To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the most cost-effective sanitation interventions for mitigating antibiotic resistance (AR), are those that reduce open defecation, or increase decentralized secondary treatment, with condomial sewerage; and 2) for Southeast Asia, the best option depends on the existing infrastructure.

(i) the incremental cost of interventions for reducing AR is a useful metric for identifying the most cost-effective sanitation interventions; (ii) in Southeast Asia, reducing OD is the most cost-effective intervention for Cambodia and East Timo, while increasing decentralized secondary treatment (with condominial sewering) is the most cost effective for Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia; and (iii) the most cost-effective interventions will vary from country to country, depending on their existing sanitation infrastructure.

1) the best approach for a country to reduce AR in wastewater will depend on the current level of development and sanitation provision; and 2) the best option is to increase decentralized secondary treatment, with condomial sewers, for countries with a sewer infrastructure; or to reduce open defecation for countries with no sewer infrastructure.
